# The hell is wrong this wednesday, The "4" incident and 12-year old php vulnerability.

So well, it's only wednesday and yeah a nice day to start it.

---

## The "4" incident

Let's start with the "4" incident, The private key for one of eMudhra's intermidiate CAs was the number 4. No I am serious the key was 4. Anyone could guess it in seconds, forge any website's certificate, and impersonate banks, email or google.com or anyother. Google, Mozilla, Apple and and Microsoft blocked the certs, and eMudhra revoked them, but old devices and software that don't check revocation lists might still be living in the past.

---

### How did this happen?

Back in April 2025, eMudra ran a key generation cermony for a batch of 24 intermidiate CA keys. The script was supposed to generate massive random numbers. Instead, there was a bug in the wrap and unwrap step, and it sput out a second set of week keys right alongside the normal ones.

And guess what the numbers were 4 well the popular one, then there was 56 and also 115. Bruh, mostly it's a P-384 private key. To make matters worse, the weak key files had labels super similar to the normal ones. Staff picked the weak ones and used them to sign certificates, like bruhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhhh.

And nobody noticed for a year, until October 2026 Wayne stumbled on it while scanning public certificate data. He signed a test message with the weak keys, proved anyone could forge signatures and reported it. Then others followed and recovered all the private keys from public certs in less than a second.

![bruh](https://media1.tenor.com/m/T1zotsnaPJsAAAAd/bruh-meme.gif)

---

### So like what's the maths?

eMudhra used Elliptic Curve Cryptography with the P-384 curve. The 384 means the numbers should normally be 384 bits long. On the curve, there is a string point called the generator point G. Everyone knows G, it is public and part of the standard. Your private key d is supposed to be a massive random 384-but number. But yeah nah you know let me do it 4.

The public key Q is calculated using scalar multiplication:

Q= d * G

This does not mean regular multiplication, it means taking point G and adding it to itsled d times:

If d = 1, Q = G
If d = 2, Q = 2G
If d = 3, Q = 3G
If d = 4, Q = 4G

Yeap 4G, normally if Q and G was given, finding d is the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem, impossible to crack for 384-bit number because no one can count that high. But when this nigga d = 4, yeah. This is ragebaiting at this point, anyone can do it.

The OpenSSL commands flaoting around X,are just extracting the public key from the cert, hashing it, and deriving the public key from the private key 4 to see if the hashes match. An Scott Helme put it, nobody stole anything, this key has been effectively public since day one. Bro said it like this shit was normal.

![You ...](https://media1.tenor.com/m/F0-yo8vuIJMAAAAd/maya-higa.gif)

---

### Why this is bad?

A CA's private key is the ultimate master stamp. If you know the private key is 4, you can create a fake certificate for google.com or another, sign it with 4, and browsers will show a green padlock even though you are talking straight to a low ball sweaty ass hacker who haven't got up from his chair for the last month.

Or your local scammer in your cafe will do a man-in-the-middle attack, intercept traffic, steal passwords, and spy on your secret love life which is consisted of another scammer in Mnyammar. Especially for servers that don't validate cert chains or handle revocation properly. And the scope is not small. Multiple intermediate certificates were affected for HTTPS and code signing, cross-signed by Sectigo, making the whole trust chain issue way bigger.

---

### Has It Been Fixed?

Yes... well not all, old devices, embedded systems, Java apps, and software that skips revocation checks are still living in the past. (Unfriendly reminder: macOS built-in curl might still trust them because its cert bundle doesn't check revocation info).

![I don't use macOS](https://media1.tenor.com/m/YLr1JA5iHE0AAAAd/macos-i-use-arch-btw.gif)

---

### So what you should do?

Delete that shit, why would you even use macOS.JK

Just Update that dogshit and it's browser, Play it safe and check your setup.

If you are a dev or ops person, check your stack, check whether your server uses an eMudhra chain, update your trust stores, and verify your revocation behavior. If your software doesn't check revocation, a revoked cert means nothing. (Oh shit this is also for me).

---

## The PHP attack "PHP2Shell" (CVE-2026-109618 & CVE-2026-109619): PHP’s Massive 0-Day RCE Exploit

You think the eMudhra key being 4 was bad well PHP is more baddie on this one. A 0day that was there for 12 years, how fun right?

So let's see each one:

### CVE-2026-109618 (Out-Of-Memory RCE & Data Leak):

When a request hits PHP and triggers an out-of-memory (OOM) error, PHP uses longjmp() to bail out. But because of improper cleanup, the memory stays uninitialized. Attackers can intentionally send crafted requests (like heavy multipart/form-data file uploads) to trigger OOM, manipulate that uninitialized memory, and get arbitrary code execution. On top of that, it pulls a Heartbleed-style memory leak where sensitive data (API keys, session tokens, passwords) can end up spit back into session cookies.

### CVE-2026-109619 (Stale Global State RCE):

When a fatal error hits, longjmp() leaves global memory pointing to freed memory regions. When the PHP worker process gets reused for the next request, it reads or branches on that freed memory. Boom type confusion in OPcache and remote code execution.

---

### Why mostly every PHP dev is kind of cooked?

It affects WordPress, Magento, Laravel, Showare, WooCommerce it doesn't matter if your application code is clean. The vulnerability is inside the PHP engine itself, parsing the request before your even gets to run. The exploit tool PHP2Shell allows unauthenticated attackers to fire off requests and instantly grab a shell on the underlying server. Millions of legacy servers still running end-of-life PHP 5.x and 7.x are permanently exposed because official patches are only hitting supported PHP 8.x branches.

![PHP](https://media1.tenor.com/m/gMcOX5g1sQkAAAAd/heh.gif)

---

### Has it been fixed?

Yes, official patches are dropping.

Update PHP immediately for now, if you manage your own servers, update to the latest patched PHP 8.x release right now. Application-level fixes or "maintenance mode" flags won't help because PHP processes the payload before the application code runs.

And if you can't patch immediately yeah nuke that project. Not funny I know but it is too me. lock multipart/form-data requests at your web server level (Nginx/Apache). Set your web server to only allow GET and HEAD requests. Temporarily stop PHP-FPM or take affected servers offline until patches are applied.

Bad day to be a PHP developer.

![PHP](https://media1.tenor.com/m/TDJ0PSIAHREAAAAd/he-was-forced-to-use-php-php.gif)
